newsitem.title: USA: Clinton warns of "hot spots" in emissions trading.
newsitem.headline: Clinton warns of "hot spots" in emissions trading.

text.p: The White House Monday touted the benefits of using emissions trading permits or fees as an efficient way to control pollution, but raised concern that it could create "hot spots" of harmful emissions.
The annual "Economic Report of the President" said allowing polluters to trade emissions permits spurred them to trim pollution in the cheapest ways possible.

But at a time when the Clinton administration is weighing proposals for U.S. trading of nitrogen oxide permits and international trading of carbon emissions permits, the report warned that deciding how to distribute permits will be tough.

"A problem can arise when the damages from emissions are not distributed evenly over the geographic area in which firms can trade permits," said the report by President Bill Clinton's Council of Economic Advisers.

"If polluters with high abatement costs -- the ones most likely to buy permits -- are geographically concentrated, a 'hot spot' area that is persistently in seriously noncompliance may result," it said.
The report said hot spots could become a problem with sulfur dioxide emissions from power plants, and might be more serious with nitrogen oxides.
Nevertheless, the White House said emissions trading remained an appealing option because of the possible cost savings.

It said the Environmental Protection Agency estimated that emissions trading for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and mercury could cut emissions control costs in 2005 by almost two-thirds compared with normal regulatory requirements.

And it said that the Stanford Energy Modeling Forum had predicted that international trading of carbon emissions permits could cut costs in half compared with using only domestic pollution control programs, and by as much as 80 percent if there was some flexibility in the timing of curbing pollution.
